question_text: Why are the alkali metals not found in the free state in nature?

CONTENT CARRIED BEYOND THE PRINTED ANSWER and to be confirmed by a teacher: that sodium and potassium are kept under kerosene while lithium, whose density is about 0.53 against kerosene's 0.8, floats on it and is kept in paraffin wax. This is standard content and it is why the storage sentence names two liquids rather than one.

steps.why: The reason is the single loosely held ns¹ electron. Removing it needs very little energy, so an alkali metal reacts with the air and water around it instead of remaining as the free metal.
common_mistakes: Writing that their ionisation enthalpy is high. Each alkali metal has the lowest ionisation enthalpy in its own period, which is why they react so readily. Down the group the values fall, so lithium's is the highest of the six.
Stopping at the word reactive. Reactivity is the right reason, but add the cause — one ns¹ electron and a low ionisation enthalpy — to make it complete.
steps.memory_tip: One outer electron, lost easily, so the free metal does not last.
steps.margin_note: Name the ns¹ electron and the low ionisation enthalpy behind the reactivity.

steps.why: The second half of the answer is what follows from the reactivity: in nature these metals are held in compounds, and even a pure sample has to be kept under kerosene or wax to keep it from reacting.
common_mistakes: Writing that they are stored in water. They react with water; sodium and potassium are kept under kerosene, and lithium, which floats on kerosene, in paraffin wax.
Giving the reason but not saying where the metals are actually found — in their compounds.
steps.memory_tip: Found as compounds in nature, kept under kerosene or wax in the laboratory.
steps.margin_note: Say the combined state, then add the storage liquid as the familiar example.
